## @benradack
If your emails aren't bringing back old customers, build a winback campaign.

→ 1 CBO
→ Target your existing customer list
→ Exclude recent purchasers (last 30-90 days depending on your repeat purchase window)

The creative:

→ A new offer they haven't seen yet (discount, bundle, free shipping)
→ Or one of your newer ads they haven't been served before

Why this works.

Emails get filtered into promo tabs or spam. They get ignored. Meta ads catch your churned customers where they're already scrolling. No filter to get past.

You're hitting them before they forget about you completely.

These people already bought once. They already trust the product. Getting them back is way easier than acquiring someone new.

Low hanging fruit. Most brands ignore it.

## @benradack
Partnership ads are a huge unlock with Meta ads.

You can run the same ad through both your brand page and a creator page (or non-brand page) at the same time. Meta dynamically picks which entity to show based on what it thinks will perform.

Why this works.

It's not really about reaching new people (though it can help if the page has followers). It's about making your ads feel more authentic.

→ An ad from your brand page feels like an ad
→ The same ad from a creator page or niche page feels like content

How I run it.

→ Create a whitelisting CBO
→ One ad set per page so I can track which entity is pulling weight
→ Partnership ads turned on so each ad runs from the connected page
→ Min spend limits on newer pages so Meta gives them a fair shot

Same top performing ad, different page, often a completely different result. I've seen ads that did fine on the brand page absolutely crush from a creator or tastemaker page.

## @sarahlevinger
When it comes to getting a sale, there is no such thing as “simple math” in the mind of the customer.

It may seem like their decision comes down to: “do I want this? Yes.” But the brain is actually doing an enormous amount of calculations in the background, all of which have an effect on whether this person acts on that desire or not:

- Do I need this?
- Where will I store this? 
- Have I tried this before?
- Do I already have this at home?
- Do I like this flavor (variation etc)
- Do I have enough money for this?
- Who else do I know that has this?
- What will it say about it me if I buy?

It’s bad practice to assume the only thing your customer needs is to be convinced. Thats only step 1.
